rv.q: His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story.
Lucian Msamati anchors this ambitious, overstretched story of Afrofuturist ambition

It’s a measure of the strength of the production (co-directed by Cameron, with Monique Touko) that we buy into the idea that deep African spirit – even superstition – can help propel scientific enquiry.

Camus famously opined that 'The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man's heart' and Msamati's driven (but not deranged) Nkoloso manages to make it feel like the dream is more important than the truth. He inspires a mixed-sex generation of Zambians to believe that they are destined for bigger things.
The Afronauts is a funny, bruising and beautifully realised play that earns its running time and then some.
It proves accessible, in places enlightening, and a surprisingly entertaining vehicle despite the deployment of a little historical licence and a slightly overlong first half.
Our problem with it is that it needs a good edit currently and to lose at least half an hour before the doubtless fascinating story at its heart can be emphasised with the clarity it deserves.

cn.t: Critics find *The Afronauts* a worthy, thought-provoking follow-up to Cameron's acclaimed *For Black Boys…*, with strong performances earning solid marks — though its ambitious 190-minute runtime may test some patience.
